t.7.80.1: Having heard of the origin of the Kimpuruṣas, Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata then both said to Rāma, the lord of the people, "It is a wonder!"
t.7.80.2: Then the greatly renowned Rāma, whose soul was devoted to dharma, went on once more to narrate this tale of the son of Prajāpati.
t.7.80.3: Seeing all those kiṃnarīs fled away, the best of sages, as if smiling, spoke to that woman endowed with beauty.
t.7.80.4: O lady of lovely face, I am the dearly beloved son of Soma. O fair-hipped one, accept me with devotion and with an affectionate eye.
t.7.80.5: Hearing those words of his, Ilā, alone in that deserted place and bereft of her own people, replied to the great planet, whose appearance was exceedingly lovely.
t.7.80.6: O gentle one, I am yours, ready to do whatever you desire and subject to your will. Command me, O son of Soma, and do as you wish.
t.7.80.7: Hearing that wondrous-seeming speech of hers, the son of Candramas, filled with joy and full of desire, made love with her.
t.7.80.8: For Budha, the amorous one, as he delighted exceedingly in that lovely-faced Ilā, the month of Mādhava passed as if it were but a moment.
t.7.80.9: Then, when the month was complete, the glorious son of Prajāpati, whose face was like the full moon, awoke upon his bed.
t.7.80.10: There he saw the son of Soma practicing austerities in a lake, his arms raised aloft and without any support, and the king addressed him.
t.7.80.11: O Lord, I entered the inaccessible mountain together with my followers, yet I do not see that army. Where, then, have those men of mine gone?
t.7.80.13: Your servants were struck down by a great shower of stones, and you, afflicted with fear of the wind and rain, lay asleep in the hermitage.
t.7.80.12: Having heard those words spoken by the royal sage, who had lost his awareness, he gave an auspicious reply, consoling him with the most excellent speech.
t.7.80.14: Take heart, may good fortune be with you; fearless and free from distress, O hero, live here as you please, eating fruits and roots.
t.7.80.15: Comforted by those words, that greatly renowned king, though dejected at the destruction of his servants, replied with an auspicious speech.
t.7.80.16: I shall give up my own kingdom, but I could not live even for a moment deprived of my servants, O brahmin; please grant me your permission.
t.7.80.17: O Brahman, my eldest son, devoted to dharma and of great renown, is known as Śaśabindu; he will succeed to my kingdom.
t.7.80.18: For, O one of great splendor, having gone back, I shall not be able to speak even a single inauspicious word to the wives of my servants, who are living in happiness.
t.7.80.19: As the lord of kings spoke thus, Budha then soothingly said something most wonderful: "May your stay here be pleasing to you."
t.7.80.20: You should not grieve, O mighty son of Kardama; when you have dwelt here for a year, I shall bring about what is good for you.
t.7.80.21: Having heard those words of Budha, whose deeds were unwearied, words spoken by that expounder of the Veda, he set his mind on dwelling there.
t.7.80.22: For one month he, having then become a woman, a lovely one, gave delight unceasingly; for the next month, in the state of a man, he set his mind upon dharma.
t.7.80.23: Then, in the ninth month, that fair-hipped Ilā gave birth to Purūravas, the son of Soma's son, her own child.
t.7.80.24: As soon as he was born, the fair-hipped lady placed Ilā's mighty son, whose complexion matched Budha's own, in the hand of his father.
t.7.80.25: Budha too, self-possessed, comforted the king who had become a man again, and delighted him with discourses filled with dharma.
